title: Daimler, Maybach and the First Mercedes
summary: In a garden summer house near Stuttgart, two inventors worked so secretly that the neighbours thought they were making fake money! Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach built a small, fast engine, a wooden motorbike and a carriage with no horse. Later a racing fan named his new super-fast car after his daughter, who was only about 11: Mercedes.

sections.heading: The Gunsmith and the Orphan
paragraphs: Our story now moves about 100 kilometres south-east of Mannheim, to the kingdom of Württemberg and its capital, Stuttgart. Here lived two men who, in the very same years as Karl Benz, were trying to build a light, fast engine that could move a vehicle. They were Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach, and their partnership is one of the great double acts of engineering history.

Gottlieb Daimler was born on 17 March 1834 in Schorndorf, a small town east of Stuttgart, the son of a baker. He trained first as a gunsmith, passing his trade exam in 1852, which taught him to work metal with great precision. Then he studied engineering at technical schools in Stuttgart and worked in factories in Alsace. From 1861 to 1863 he lived in England, which was then the world's leading industrial country, and worked for engineering companies including Beyer, Peacock and Company, a famous builder of railway locomotives in Manchester. He came home full of ideas about machines and mass production.

Wilhelm Maybach had a much harder start. He was born on 9 February 1846 in Heilbronn, the son of a carpenter. His mother died when he was eight and his father two years later, leaving him an orphan. He was taken in by the Bruderhaus in Reutlingen, a charitable home founded by the pastor Gustav Werner that cared for poor children and trained them in workshops. There Maybach learned technical drawing and design, and there, in the 1860s, he met Daimler, who was working for the Bruderhaus's engineering works. Daimler spotted the quiet teenager's talent, and from then on the two worked together for most of their lives.

In 1872 Daimler became factory manager of Gasmotoren-Fabrik Deutz near Cologne, the company of Nicolaus Otto and Eugen Langen that you met in Part 3, and he brought Maybach with him as chief designer. They helped turn Otto's four-stroke engine into a reliable product. But Daimler and Otto clashed. Otto's company wanted big, slow engines for factories, while Daimler dreamed of small engines light enough to power vehicles. By 1882 Daimler had left Deutz, taking a large payment as compensation, and Maybach soon followed him.

sections.heading: The Secret Workshop in the Garden
paragraphs: Daimler bought a villa in Cannstatt, a spa town on the river Neckar just outside Stuttgart. In the garden stood a roomy summer house with glass windows, the kind of greenhouse-like building where a wealthy family might drink tea on a sunny afternoon. Daimler added a brick extension and turned it into a workshop. There, from 1882, he and Maybach worked in great secrecy, often late into the night.

All that hammering, clanking and late-night lamplight made the neighbours suspicious. According to Daimler's biographers, they reported the two men to the police as possible counterfeiters, people who make fake money. One day, while Daimler and Maybach were away, the police borrowed a key from the gardener and searched the workshop. Instead of printing presses and false coins, they found only engine parts. The story shows how strange this new kind of work looked to ordinary people in the 1880s.

Daimler and Maybach's goal was simple to say and hard to do: make the engine faster, smaller and lighter. A big part of the problem was ignition. Lighting the fuel at exactly the right moment, over and over, was tricky. Otto's engines used a flame and sliding valves, which limited how fast they could run. Daimler and Maybach used a 'hot tube': a small metal tube, closed at one end, that poked into the cylinder and was kept glowing hot from the outside by a little burner. When the piston squeezed the fuel-air mixture into the hot tube, it caught fire. It was a crude system, and burners could blow out or set things alight, but it allowed the engine to run much faster.

In 1885 they finished an engine that was small enough to carry. It stood upright, with a single cylinder, inside a tall casing, and because of its shape people nicknamed it the 'Standuhr', which means grandfather clock. It ran on petroleum spirit and turned at about 600 revolutions per minute. That might not sound fast compared with a modern car engine, but earlier gas engines typically ran at only about 120 to 180 revolutions per minute. Faster running meant more power from a smaller, lighter engine. The grandfather clock engine is often seen as an ancestor of the modern petrol engine.

sections.heading: A Riding Car and a Carriage Without a Horse
paragraphs: To test the new engine, Daimler and Maybach built a vehicle around it in 1885. They called it the Reitwagen, which means riding car. It was made mostly of wood, with a wooden frame, wooden wheels with iron tyres, and no springs at all. The engine sat in the middle, beneath the leather saddle. Its single cylinder had a volume of 264 cubic centimetres and produced about half a horsepower, driving the back wheel with a belt. Because the riders were worried about balance, it had two small spring-loaded side wheels, like the training wheels on a child's bicycle.

In November 1885, Daimler's 16-year-old son Paul rode the Reitwagen a few kilometres from Cannstatt to Untertürkheim, reaching around 11 to 12 kilometres per hour. It was not a comfortable ride. The hot tube ignition sat right under the seat, and accounts say the seat caught fire. Even so, the Reitwagen is often called the first motorcycle, or at least the first motorcycle with a petrol-burning internal combustion engine. Some historians question the title, since it had those extra side wheels and steam-powered two-wheelers had been tried earlier. Daimler himself saw it only as a test bed and soon moved on. The original was destroyed in a fire in 1903, but replicas can be seen today in the Mercedes-Benz Museum in Stuttgart, the Deutsches Museum in Munich and elsewhere.

Next, in 1886, Daimler bought a four-wheeled horse carriage made by the coachbuilders Wilhelm Wimpff and Son. To avoid gossip, he told the neighbours it was a birthday present for his wife. Then he and Maybach removed the shafts where a horse would be harnessed, strengthened the carriage and fitted a larger version of their engine. The result looked exactly like what it was: a carriage with the horse missing. It is reported to have been the first four-wheeled vehicle to reach about 16 kilometres per hour.

Notice the difference between Daimler's approach and Benz's. Karl Benz, as you saw in Part 4, designed his Patent-Motorwagen as one complete new machine. Daimler and Maybach, at first, were mainly interested in the engine. They put it into almost anything that could move: the Reitwagen, a carriage, a motorboat and even an early airship. Their idea was that the engine itself was the invention, and that it could power the world. In 1889 they did build a more car-like vehicle with steel wheels and a light frame influenced by bicycles, the Stahlradwagen, and showed it in Paris. It was not produced in Germany, but it was licensed to be built in France, which turned out to be very important.

Here is one of the oddest facts in the history of the car. Benz in Mannheim and Daimler in Cannstatt were working on the same idea at the same time, only about 100 kilometres apart, and yet they apparently never met. There is no good evidence that they knew each other during the years of invention. Even when their companies fought a patent case in Mannheim in 1896, the two men are said not to have met. Their firms were rivals for 40 years, and they would only come together long after Daimler's death.

sections.heading: German Engines, French Cars
paragraphs: In the early 1890s the place where the car business really took off was not Germany but France. French roads were generally good, many wealthy people loved new gadgets, and Paris was full of engineers and bicycle makers looking for the next big thing. Daimler's engines reached France through a Belgian lawyer named Edouard Sarazin, who represented Daimler's interests there. When Sarazin died in 1887, Daimler asked his widow, Louise Sarazin, to carry on the agency, and she did so with great skill. She arranged for the French engineering firm Panhard et Levassor to build Daimler engines under licence. A licence is permission, usually paid for, to use someone else's patented invention. In 1890 Louise Sarazin married Émile Levassor, one of the firm's two partners.

Panhard et Levassor, run by René Panhard and Émile Levassor, made woodworking machines in Paris. Levassor first tried Daimler engines in vehicles of various shapes, and the company sold its first car in 1890. Then, in 1891, Levassor made a decision that shaped almost every car for the next hundred years. He put the engine at the front of the car, under a bonnet, with a clutch behind it, then a gearbox with sliding gears, and then a drive to the rear wheels. The driver sat behind the engine.

This arrangement became known as the Système Panhard, the Panhard system. Why was it so good? Putting the heavy engine at the front placed weight over the steering wheels, which made the car steadier. It left room for passengers behind, made it easy to reach the engine for repairs, and allowed a longer, roomier body. The gearbox let the driver choose different gears for hills and flat roads. Levassor is said to have described his first sliding-gear gearbox as 'brutal but it works', a remark that shows how rough the early versions were. Over the following decades, nearly every carmaker in the world adopted the same basic layout, and many cars still use a front engine with rear-wheel drive today.

The second French company to use Daimler engines was Peugeot. The Peugeot family had been making things in eastern France since 1810: first saws and steel tools, then coffee grinders, pepper mills, steel ribs for the hooped crinoline skirts of the 1850s, and, from around 1880, bicycles. Armand Peugeot was fascinated by vehicles. In 1889 Peugeot built a three-wheeled steam car designed by Léon Serpollet, but only four were made. In 1890 Peugeot switched to a four-wheeled petrol car using a Daimler-type engine built by Panhard. Six years later, in 1896, Peugeot began making its own engines, and Armand founded a separate car company. Today Peugeot is one of the oldest car brands in the world.

So in a strange way, Germany invented the engines and France turned them into a car industry. By the late 1890s France was the world's leading car-making country, and its races, which you will read about in Part 15, made Panhard and Peugeot famous.

sections.heading: Troubles at Daimler's Company
paragraphs: Back in Cannstatt, Daimler needed money to grow. In 1890 he founded the Daimler-Motoren-Gesellschaft, or DMG, meaning Daimler Motor Company, with Maybach as chief designer. To raise money, the company took on powerful investors, especially the industrialists Max von Duttenhofer and Wilhelm Lorenz, who had made their fortunes in gunpowder and ammunition. Daimler disliked turning his firm into a company run by shareholders, and he was soon outvoted.

The new bosses wanted to make money quickly by selling stationary engines, while Daimler and Maybach wanted to develop vehicles. Maybach was refused a seat on the board and left in 1891, though Daimler secretly kept paying him to continue designing. Working in a hotel ballroom in Cannstatt, Maybach produced two of his most important inventions. In 1893 he patented the spray-nozzle carburetor, which used the rush of air into the engine to suck fuel through a tiny jet and break it into a fine mist, rather like a perfume spray. That kind of carburetor would be used in cars for most of the twentieth century. In 1894 Daimler, Maybach and Daimler's son Paul designed the Phoenix engine, which became the company's main product.

Daimler himself was squeezed out in 1893, selling his shares. Then help came from an unexpected direction. Frederick Simms, a German-born friend of Daimler's who had set up a Daimler business in Britain, agreed to pay a large sum for the British rights to Daimler's patents, but only on condition that Daimler be brought back into DMG. In 1894 and 1895 both Daimler and Maybach returned. It shows how much the new industry depended on a few gifted people and on the friendships between them.

sections.heading: Monsieur Mercedes
paragraphs: Now we need to travel to the sunny coast of the Mediterranean, to the city of Nice in the south of France, where rich people from all over Europe spent the winter. Here lived Emil Jellinek, born in 1853 in Leipzig, the son of Adolf Jellinek, a famous rabbi in Vienna. Emil had been a diplomat for Austria-Hungary in North Africa and had worked in insurance, and he had become wealthy. In Nice he sold cars to rich clients, and in 1896 he bought his first Daimler car. He soon became one of DMG's most important customers and dealers.

Jellinek loved speed. He entered races along the Riviera, and like many racers of the time he used a nickname instead of his real name. The name he chose was Mercedes, after his daughter, Mercédès Jellinek, who was born in Vienna on 16 September 1889. Mercedes is a Spanish girl's name that means 'mercies' or 'mercy'. His racing team became known by the same name.

Jellinek was not shy about telling DMG what he wanted. The early Daimler cars were tall and top-heavy, more like motorized carriages, and they were dangerous at speed. After a fatal crash involving a Daimler car in a hill climb race near Nice in 1900, Jellinek pushed for something completely different: a car that was lower, longer, lighter and more powerful. In 1900 he made DMG an offer that was hard to refuse. He reportedly agreed to buy 36 cars for around half a million marks, an enormous sum, if the cars were built to his ideas and sold under the name Mercedes in France and some other countries.

So, just to be clear: the famous name Mercedes does not come from Daimler or Benz or anyone in their families. It comes from a girl of about 11, the daughter of a car fan in Nice. Funnily enough, the real Mercédès never shared her father's passion for cars. She was a musician with a fine singing voice, and she is said never to have owned a car herself.

sections.heading: The First Modern Car: the Mercedes 35 hp
paragraphs: Wilhelm Maybach, with help from Paul Daimler, designed the new car. The first one was delivered to Jellinek in Nice in December 1900, and it became known as the Mercedes 35 hp, after its engine power of 35 PS (German horsepower, almost exactly the same as 35 horsepower). It looked completely different from the horseless carriages of a few years earlier.

First, it was low. The frame was made of pressed steel, steel sheets stamped into strong U-shaped beams, instead of wood or steel tubes. The engine sat low down over the front axle, and the car's centre of gravity was much lower, so it was far less likely to tip over in corners. The wheelbase, the distance between front and rear wheels, was long, which made it more stable at speed.

Second, it was powerful. The engine had four cylinders and a capacity of about 5.9 litres, more than six times the size of the engine in Benz's first Motorwagen. It produced its 35 horsepower at about 950 revolutions per minute. Maybach used light metals: the crankcase was made of aluminium. Instead of the old hot tubes, the engine used a magneto, a small generator that made its own electric current for the ignition sparks, so there were no flames to blow out.

Third, it could keep cool. Maybach's honeycomb radiator, which he had patented in 1897, had about 8,000 thin tubes through which air could flow, giving a huge surface for heat to escape from the cooling water. Water went round and round in a closed system instead of boiling away. Compare this with the evaporative cooling of Bertha Benz's Motorwagen, which had to be refilled every few kilometres. The radiator sat right at the front, giving the Mercedes its famous face.

Fourth, it was easy to drive fast. A gear lever moved in a metal 'gate' with slots for four forward gears and reverse, a design that made changing gear more precise. The car weighed about 1,200 kilograms, and the racing versions could reach about 86 kilometres per hour.

Success did not come instantly. In January 1901 the new cars were entered in a race at Pau in south-western France, and technical problems put them out after only a few laps. Maybach and the DMG engineers went back to work on the faults, and a few weeks later they were ready for a much bigger test.

In March 1901, at the 'Nice Week' of motor races, the Mercedes cars, partly driven by Wilhelm Werner, astonished everyone. They won race after race, and in the hill climb from Nice to La Turbie they set a record average speed of about 51 kilometres per hour, reaching about 86 kilometres per hour at top speed. A French motoring writer, Paul Meyan, is reported to have said: 'We have entered the Mercedes era.' Other carmakers quickly began copying its design. That is why many historians call the 1901 Mercedes 35 hp the first modern car: its low pressed-steel frame, front engine, honeycomb radiator and gate gearchange set the pattern for decades to come.

Just think how far things had moved in only fifteen years. Benz's first Motorwagen of 1886 had about three-quarters of a horsepower and a top speed of about 16 kilometres per hour. The 1901 Mercedes had around 35 horsepower, nearly fifty times as much, and could go five or six times as fast. The Motorwagen looked like a tricycle; the Mercedes looked like a car. The horseless carriage had become a machine with a shape of its own, and once people had seen it, there was no going back.

sections.heading: From Mercedes to Mercedes-Benz
paragraphs: Sadly, Gottlieb Daimler never saw this triumph. He had suffered from heart trouble for years, and he died in Cannstatt on 6 March 1900, aged 65, before the first Mercedes was finished. His son Paul and Wilhelm Maybach carried on the work. In June 1902 DMG registered Mercedes as its trademark for cars. In 1903 Emil Jellinek legally changed his own name to Jellinek-Mercedes and joked that this was probably the first time a father had taken his daughter's name.

The company went through dramatic times. On 10 June 1903 a great fire burned down the old Cannstatt factory, destroying machines and 93 finished Mercedes cars, and production moved to a big new factory in Untertürkheim nearby. Maybach finally left DMG in 1907 after the company gave him an unimportant role. He went on to build engines for Zeppelin airships and, after World War I, luxury cars under his own name. He died in 1929. In 1909 DMG adopted its famous three-pointed star as a trademark. According to the company's story, it went back to Gottlieb Daimler's dream of engines for land, water and air.

After World War I Germany suffered a terrible economic crisis, with money losing its value almost by the hour. DMG built only 1,020 vehicles in 1923 and even made bicycles and typewriters to survive. Its old rival, Benz & Cie. in Mannheim, was struggling too. In 1924 the two firms signed an agreement to work together, and on 28 June 1926 they merged to form Daimler-Benz. Their cars were given a new brand that joined the two histories: Mercedes-Benz. Karl Benz, by then in his eighties, sat on the board of the new company until his death in 1929. The rivals who had never met were now one company.
Mercédès Jellinek died in Vienna in February 1929 at the age of 39. The girl who never owned a car had given her name to one of the most famous car brands on Earth.

Yet if you had travelled back to the streets of New York, Paris or London around 1900, just as the first Mercedes was being built, you might have been surprised by what you saw. Many of the motor cars gliding past were not petrol cars at all. Some hummed along almost silently, powered by electric batteries. Others puffed clouds of white vapour, because they ran on steam. In many cities, those quiet electric and steam cars were the most popular kind of all. The great race between steam, electricity and petrol was only just beginning.

deepDive: Who deserves credit for the modern car? The Daimler-Maybach story shows why historians avoid naming a single inventor. Benz designed the first complete, patented petrol car in 1886. Daimler and Maybach, working independently in Cannstatt, focused on a light, high-speed engine: the 1885 'grandfather clock' engine ran at about 600 revolutions per minute, several times faster than the roughly 120 to 180 rpm of earlier gas engines. Because power is roughly the force on the piston multiplied by how often it fires, a faster engine can give more power from less weight, and that power-to-weight ratio is what made engines practical for vehicles, boats and, later, aircraft. Their hot-tube ignition was a stepping stone; by 1901 the Mercedes used a low-voltage magneto, and in 1902 Bosch's high-voltage magneto and spark plug (Part 8) set the standard. Many key steps were French. Panhard et Levassor's 1891 layout, with the engine in front driving the rear wheels through a clutch and sliding-gear gearbox, became the template for most cars for the next century. Historians also emphasise Louise Sarazin, who negotiated the French licences after her husband's death in 1887 and is one of several women, like Bertha Benz, whose business roles were long overlooked. The claim that the 1901 Mercedes 35 hp was 'the first modern car' is a judgement, not a measurable fact. Supporters point to its combination of features: a pressed-steel frame, a low centre of gravity, a 5.9-litre four-cylinder engine with an aluminium crankcase, a honeycomb radiator with thousands of tubes in a closed cooling system and a gate gearchange. Critics note that each feature had appeared somewhere before; what was new was putting them together in one well-balanced, fast and reliable package. The business story matters too. Emil Jellinek's large order, reportedly 36 cars for around half a million marks, gave DMG the money and confidence to build a radical design, an early example of a customer shaping a product. The 1926 merger that created Daimler-Benz was driven by the post-war economic crisis rather than friendship: both firms were weak, and combining design, production and sales helped them survive.
funFact: The first person to ride Daimler's 1885 Reitwagen, often called the first motorcycle, was his 16-year-old son Paul, and the seat reportedly caught fire because the hot ignition tube sat right under it.

check.q: Whose name did the Mercedes car get?
check.a: Mercédès Jellinek, the daughter of Emil Jellinek
